hypotheses:
iaso works in any repository and for any coding agent: one host-neutral core does the work, and each host gets a thin adapter that installs only that host's own things. The Claude Code plugin installs only Claude Code's command, skills, checks and panels, and the Codex and Hermes adapters likewise install only their own. Adopting a repository is one plain request that changes nothing the second time, and where iaso is not adopted it stays silent apart from one line. iaso is built with iaso.
will: One host-neutral core that every coding agent's adapter feeds, so the same session gives the same agent context, owner lines and block on every host, with a no-hook fallback the agent runs.
will: A Claude Code plugin that carries its own copy of iaso and installs only Claude Code's command, skills, background checks and panels.
will: Thin adapters for Codex and Hermes, kept for later and not frozen, each writing only its own host's files, keeping your own entries and removing only iaso's; the Pi adapter and the MCP server are removed and come back later only if needed.
will: Adoption of any repository on a plain request or /iaso init, idempotent, with one line and nothing else where iaso is not adopted; projects set up the old way keep working and move to the plugin on request.
will: iaso developed with iaso: its own repository adopted like any other, its commits naming the requirement they serve.
won't: Install anything for one host when iaso is set up for another, or copy Claude Code's command, skills or checks into a project.
won't: Run the project's own development setup of iaso from the plugin.
won't: Ask you to type a shell or install command, or a record id.
won't: Claim a host's adapter is active when it has only written its files.
won't: Depend on pi-agent-factory at run time.

# iaso: owner intent brief (authoritative)

This file records the owner's intent from the 2026-10-05 brainstorming conversation. Every iaso artifact and implementation choice must respect it. Quotes are verbatim.

## Purpose (verbatim)
- "the goal of coherence tooling is to ensure the alignment between user's intent and understanding of what he wants to build and the current state of the system being built."
- "I find that the main issue with current coding agents is that we either have to micro manage them or 'vibe code / Spec driven develop' the thing. I'd like coherence to make vibe coding grounded on the projects artifacts in an efficient, reliable and trustable manner."
- On pi-agent-factory's governed workflows: "they seem pretty heavy, and also quite orthogonal to the developments claude and other coding agents are doing ... whether that really makes sense to have those heavy blackboxed workflows in the first place. isnt there a more elegant way of doing things nowadays? ... a lighter, more elegant and interactive way to leverage coherence."
- On planning: "Don't you think that we'd need planning features still? how do you ensure that people defining their system will have their intent succesfully translated?"

## Decisions the owner made (Q -> answer)
1. Audience: "A / B". iaso is a standalone tool installable in any repository (A), and it is designed so pi-agent-factory can later migrate its artifacts onto it (B).
2. Planning mode: "C". Incremental intent capture is the default. Large, risky or cross-cutting work escalates to an explicit up-front spec the owner approves. The same artifacts serve both modes, and the tool suggests when to escalate.
   Intent-translation mechanisms agreed in the conversation:
   - read-back in the user's own terms (what will and won't be done, assumptions labelled);
   - requirements anchored in concrete examples the user confirms (given/when/then, including edge cases), which become acceptance tests;
   - ambiguity surfaced as explicit decisions ("I assumed A; B also fits");
   - traceable links: intent -> requirement -> examples/tests -> code;
   - a living record kept honest by drift signals.
3. Hosts: "B. I guess the CLI / lib can be re-used from pi-agent-factory?" A host-neutral core (CLI + library) with thin adapters. Claude Code ships first; Codex, Pi, Hermes and MCP come later. Reuse pi-agent-factory code by EXTRACTION, not forking: copy selected modules with their tests and simplify them. Do NOT bring the per-turn admission/coordination weight.
4. Artifacts: "B. can be the way to go but be careful about loosing some important features, for example the hash is important for staleness detection." A new, simpler record model with a pi-agent-factory importer. Familiar IDs and conventions are kept: FEAT-###, SR-###, NC-####, and `SR:` commit trailers.
   Owner-confirmed KEEP list ("Keep list looks fine"):
   - content hashes and staleness on records and links (each link pins the hashes of both ends; a change on either end makes it stale);
   - approvals pinned to exact content (simplified consent);
   - append-only evidence and decision records;
   - `SR:` commit trailers and claims checks (claimed vs declared paths);
   - relation validation (no dangling links);
   - nonconformances (NCs) as first-class records;
   - feature grouping (bundles);
   - test evidence pinned to the code and environment identity, plus the failure policy (flaky rerun on the same tree; owner-waiver targeted rerun; a full rerun only when shared test infrastructure changes);
   - advisory fidelity judging, scoped to changed requirements.
   DROP or defer: the planning run state machine, consent phrases, manifests and handoff hashes, review swarms, and governed execution as the default.
5. Interaction: "A". Mostly in the background: a status-line indicator, a short alignment summary at the end of each turn, and questions ONLY on a real intent change (a request that contradicts or extends a confirmed requirement), an unconfirmed decision that matters, or a regression. Everything else is logged for on-demand reading.
6. First scope: "Would be nice to dogfood the version to itself as soon as possible and build with it." The first sub-project is core + grounding loop + covering-test verification, built so that iaso is used to develop iaso from day one.
7. "think of re-using the existing artifacts no? SRs FEATs..? It's up to you." Formats and IDs are compatible; the importer reads pi-agent-factory's register (requirements/SR-*.md, docs/features/FEAT-*.md, bundles/*.json, docs/nonconformances/NC-*.md).
8. JEV: "what about JEV development work? I think it might be usefull to integrate it in this new version too?" JEV (TypeSafe's fast typed-judgment model: Choice/Score/Noul, 70-500 ms) is an OPTIONAL judgment backend for the background loop: intent-change detection, drift triage and a cheap scoped fidelity score, handing off to an LLM when confidence is low (the cascade pattern). The tool must work without it. Source design: C:/coding/pi-agent-factory/docs/coherence/specs/2026-09-28-jev-review-integration-design.md. The judgment code is in C:/coding/pi-agent-factory/src/substrate/judgment. Related intent capture work: C:/coding/pi-agent-factory/docs/coherence/specs/2026-09-29-intent-confirmed-fast-track-design.md.
9. "consider stopping developments on pi-agent-factory if it takes too much RAM". pi-agent-factory goes into maintenance mode after the current integration batch lands; new feature work moves to iaso. A fork plan is required.
10. "Consider spawning a workflow ... to capture this intent in a concept spec that we will then be able to refer to in the future, and then also plan for the work needed for dogfooding and the kind of pi-agent-factory fork that is about to happen."
11. "I wont review the concept spec or any plan. use agents that verify that my intent based on that conversation is respected. I want to have the implementation available by tomorrow morning (in 9 hours)."
12. Name: "coherence is a bit confusing because it's a usefull word to use." The repository and CLI are named `iaso` (a iaso line checks true alignment). It lives at C:/coding/iaso.

## Evidence the design draws on (from the research step)
- TDAD (arXiv 2603.17973): a grep-able test map plus a ~20-line skill cut regressions about 70%. Procedural TDD instructions WITHOUT naming which tests to check made regressions worse. Context over procedure.
- Intent continuity: extract requirements as structured records, verify which are still current, drop superseded ones, and compile only the current intent into the agent's context.
- ReqToCode: traceability as a structural, statically checkable property, with bidirectional change detection (drift).
- Lightweight spec-driven development (OpenSpec, skills as small specs, GSD) is favoured over heavy frameworks. The sweet spot is "spec-anchored": specs and code evolve together and tests enforce the alignment.
- The Claude Code primitives: CLAUDE.md for always-true facts, skills for on-demand procedures, hooks for guarantees, MCP for connections, and a status line.

## Non-negotiable quality bar
- Per-turn overhead is seconds, not minutes. A full test suite runs only at merge boundaries.
- Everything stays inspectable: plain markdown and JSON in git, with no hidden state the user cannot read.
- Trust comes from evidence: hashes, pinned approvals, test evidence pinned to identity, and append-only logs.
- Efficient for the owner: few, meaningful interruptions.

## Owner-proxy rulings (binding; added 2026-10-05 after concept verification)
The owner delegated reviews to agents. The coordinating session resolved these design tensions inside the owner's decisions. Treat them as settled, not as findings.
R1. Read-back and example confirmation are NON-BLOCKING. The read-back and proposed examples appear in the end-of-turn summary with status `proposed`. The owner confirms them in one line whenever they choose. They become a QUESTION only under the "unconfirmed decision that matters" trigger: when work relies on them at a merge boundary, for an escalated spec, or because of a contradiction. At the merge boundary, every requirement touched by the change MUST be confirmed. This reconciles intent translation (decision 2) with interaction A (decision 5).
R2. There is no "no-objection" approval. A confirmation requires the owner's explicit words. Approvals the agent records on the owner's behalf are marked `agent-relayed` and carry the owner's verbatim quote and the digest of the prompt it came from (logged by the prompt hook). The merge boundary lists agent-relayed approvals for a quick owner glance. The trust model is stated honestly: hash-chained and tamper-evident, not tamper-proof against a malicious agent.
R3. A regression means a test that previously PASSED with recorded evidence and now fails. A new test that starts red (the test-first step) is never a regression and never interrupts.
R4. Advisory fidelity without JEV: `iaso fidelity <SR>` builds a scoped packet (the requirement, its examples, linked code and test evidence) for the HOST agent to judge. It is on demand, or listed at the merge boundary, and always advisory. JEV, when available, only makes the scoring faster and cheaper.
R5. Changes to shared test infrastructure (pyproject.toml, uv.lock, conftest.py, the test plugin) never trigger a per-turn full run. They set the status to `full verification pending`, which is satisfied at the next merge boundary. Per-turn checks always run covering tests within a time budget; unknown coverage gives a bounded sample plus a pending flag.
R6. The concept's decision table must include decisions 10 and 11, including "implementation available by tomorrow morning (9 hours)" and "owner does not review; agents verify".
R7. Verifier calibration: HIGH only for a genuine contradiction or omission of the owner's explicit words or decisions, or of these rulings. A design refinement, a missing detail or a better alternative is MEDIUM at most. Do not reopen these rulings.


Question: Your brief says "Claude Code ships first; Codex, Pi, Hermes and MCP come later." Should the Codex and Hermes adapters be frozen while Claude Code is the agent working on iaso, and should the MCP server be removed rather than kept for later?

You said on 2026-10-05: "Claude Code ships first; Codex, Pi, Hermes and MCP come later."

Since then, the design-review work you approved has removed the MCP server and the Pi adapter.
Options: Keep Codex, Hermes and MCP for later; freeze and remove nothing (Recommended) (Codex, Hermes and MCP stay planned for later with no freeze and no removal. Nothing is frozen or removed now. Recommended: Your brief says these hosts 'come later' and does not mention freezing or removing any of them, so keeping them as later changes nothing you did not ask for.); Freeze Codex and Hermes; keep MCP for later (Codex and Hermes adapters get no work until Claude Code is no longer the agent on iaso. MCP stays planned for later.); Freeze Codex and Hermes and remove MCP (Codex and Hermes adapters get no work for now, and the MCP server is dropped from iaso altogether.)
Answer: Keep Codex, Hermes and MCP for later; freeze and remove nothing (Recommended)

Question: Your brief says iaso has one host-neutral core with thin adapters, and that Claude Code ships first while Codex, Pi, Hermes and MCP come later. Should the Codex and Hermes adapters also ignore child sessions, give the brief only once, send the alignment block at most once, and count a summary the owner never received as unseen?

You said on 2026-10-05: "Claude Code ships first; Codex, Pi, Hermes and MCP come later."
Options: Leave these rules out for now (Recommended) (Each adapter only installs and removes its own host's entries and keeps the owner's own entries. Child-session filtering, once-only briefs and unseen-summary marking are not built now. Recommended: Your brief asks only for the adapter split and for later hosts, and says nothing about these finer rules, so leaving them out adds nothing you did not ask for.); Build all of these rules (Each adapter also ignores child sessions, gives the brief once, sends the block at most once and marks unseen summaries. This adds work and rules your brief does not mention.)
Answer: Leave these rules out for now (Recommended)
